Chapter Three: Motivating the Emotional Side—Engaging Feelings for Lasting Change.
If you’ve ever wondered why logic alone rarely gets us moving, you’re not alone. Sure, our rational mind likes a good plan, but it’s our emotional side—what some folks call the elephant—that really drives us forward.
Think about it. When was the last time a spreadsheet inspired you? Probably never. But a powerful story, or a vivid image—that can stick with you for days, right? That’s because our feelings are the true engine of change.
Motivation comes from connecting change to something that actually matters to us. In organizations, this might mean sharing real stories about customers whose lives have improved thanks to a new product or service. And for you, personally, it could be about visualizing the real benefits of a healthier lifestyle—not just as some abstract goal, but in ways you can picture. Maybe it’s feeling energetic during your daily routine, or playing with your grandkids and keeping up with their boundless energy.
Of course, resistance is normal. It often shows up as fear, uncertainty, or even a sense of loss. The elephant really doesn’t like leaving its comfort zone. So, how do you help it move? One way is to shrink the change. Instead of asking for a complete overhaul, break things down into steps that actually feel doable. Those small wins help build confidence and create momentum—making your emotional side more willing to keep going.
For example, let’s say a company wants to improve safety. Instead of trying to fix everything at once, they could start by focusing on just one department, or even one specific type of incident. As people see progress, their belief in the possibility of bigger change starts to grow.
Another motivator? Cultivating a growth mindset. If you believe that skills and habits can be developed, then setbacks become just part of learning—not signs you’ve failed. That makes it easier to keep moving forward, even when the road gets bumpy.
So, how can you engage the emotional side in practical ways? Here are a few ideas:
Appeal to identity. Frame the change as part of who people are—or who they want to become—not just what they do.
Create early successes. Make those first steps super easy and rewarding, so you build momentum right from the start.
Use stories and vivid examples. Share narratives that bring the benefits of change to life and make them feel real.
When you address what your emotional side needs—reducing fear, building hope, and connecting to your values—change doesn’t just become possible. It actually starts to feel desirable. Once the elephant is on board, you’ll find the energy and persistence you need to make lasting change.
